issues.legal_issue: A temporary injunction against demolition requires a prima facie case, a balance of convenience in the applicant’s favour, and a clear possibility of irreparable injury, and cannot be granted merely on hardship where the structure is shown to be unauthorized.
material_facts: Occupants sought to restrain municipal demolition of structures, claiming that they were authorized or had existed before the applicable datum line and should therefore be tolerated.
The occupants produced no sanctioned plans or other reliable evidence showing that the structures under notice were authorized or had existed before the datum line.

Documents concerning taxation, licences, or earlier structures did not establish the age or authorization of the structures then standing; some earlier notices concerned smaller structures, while the structures in dispute had been replaced or substantially extended.
The municipal authority considered the occupants’ objections and documents before making final demolition orders, and the record did not show that those orders suffered from an infirmity.
issues.conclusion: The occupants had not established a prima facie case for temporary injunction, and hardship or the prospect of irreparable loss from demolition alone did not justify preserving structures that the evidence showed to be unauthorized.
issues.legal_principle: A temporary injunction requires a prima facie case, a balance of convenience favouring the applicant, and a clear possibility of irreparable injury; as equitable relief, it also requires conduct free from blame and an approach with clean hands. In demolition cases, irreparable loss may support preserving the status quo when a prima facie case is made out, but an injunction should not encourage or perpetuate an illegality. The Court applied section 351 of the Mumbai Municipal Corporation Act, 1888, and considered the Corporation’s circular of 11 November 1980 concerning non-residential structures existing before the applicable datum line. It relied on Wander Ltd. v. Antox India P. Ltd. (1990 Supp SCC 727) for interlocutory injunction principles and M.I. Builders Pvt. Ltd. v. Radhey Shyam Sahu (1999 (6) SCC 464) for the principle that judicial discretion cannot be used to perpetuate unauthorized construction.

predicates.demolition_injunction_proceeding: The occupants brought a proceeding seeking to restrain a public authority from demolishing structures.
predicates.no_reliable_proof_of_authorization_or_qu: The occupants did not produce reliable evidence that the structures were authorized or had the required pre-existing age for protection.
predicates.demolition_order_supported_by_record: The public authority considered the objections and available documents before ordering demolition, and the record disclosed no infirmity in that order.

issues.definition: When occupants seek to restrain demolition but cannot reliably establish authorization or qualifying age, and the demolition order is supported by the record, hardship alone does not justify a temporary injunction.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may interfere with a discretionary order granting a temporary injunction when the trial court exercised its discretion arbitrarily, capriciously, or perversely, or ignored relevant material or settled principles governing injunctions.
material_facts: The trial court granted temporary injunctions in suits challenging demolition notices, relying on claims that the structures had existed for years and on documents said to show taxation or other official recognition.
The appellate court examined the documents and found that they did not establish that the structures in dispute were authorized or existed before the applicable datum line.
The appellate court concluded that the trial court had drawn incorrect or vague inferences from the material and had granted injunctions despite the absence of material supporting a prima facie case.
The occupants challenged the appellate orders, arguing that an appellate court should not reassess material supporting a discretionary injunction merely because another view was possible.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court was justified in vacating the temporary injunctions because the trial court’s exercise of discretion lacked relevant material supporting a prima facie case; the Supreme Court declined to interfere with the appellate orders.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court does not substitute its discretion for that of the trial court merely because it might have reached a different conclusion; interference is justified where the discretion was exercised arbitrarily, capriciously, or perversely, or where settled principles or relevant material were ignored. Acting on no material includes cases where there is no relevant material or where the material as a whole cannot reasonably support the exercise of discretion. The Court relied on Wander Ltd. v. Antox India P. Ltd. (1990 Supp SCC 727) and Laxmikant V. Patel v. Chetanbhai Shah (2002 (3) SCC 65), and noted the limited scope of interference under Article 136 with discretionary injunction orders.

predicates.appeal_from_discretionary_injunction_ord: A party appealed an order granting or refusing a temporary injunction.
predicates.trial_court_relied_on_irrelevant_or_insu: The trial court based its discretionary order on material that did not establish the facts needed to justify the injunction.
predicates.appellate_review_found_no_reasonable_bas: The appellate court examined the material and found that it could not reasonably support the trial court’s exercise of discretion.

issues.definition: An appellate court may interfere with a discretionary injunction order when the trial court relied on irrelevant or insufficient material and appellate review finds no reasonable basis for that order.
